Execution commands · Decision memo

The complete cast

The tutorial loads these four dossiers with perla actor load --input case/players.json. The commands here are an alternative way to construct exactly the same content in a fresh project. Do not register the same actors a second time in an already loaded game. Sourced claims, constructed managerial backstories and assumed local constraints are labeled in each dossier.

Starbucks: protect the visit and earn back the labor

perla actor add home --name Starbucks --role home

h1 Reported history: Starbucks began in Seattle in 1971. Its evolution from a bean merchant into a coffeehouse makes the in-store experience part of the proposition, not simply a distribution expense. The strategic implication is an author inference. source.

h2 Reported financials: Q3 fiscal 2026 North America revenue was $7,395.1 million, operating income $1,008.9 million and operating margin 13.6%. These are segment figures, not pilot-store unit economics. source.

h3 Reported demand: US comparable sales increased 7.9% and comparable transactions 4.2% in Q3 fiscal 2026. This case tests sustaining growth; it does not assume that current transactions are declining. source.

h4 Reported strategy: Back to Starbucks combines staffing and scheduling investment, Smart Queue order sequencing, and restoration of the coffeehouse experience. These capabilities are public; the proposed 20% reservation is not an announced policy. source.

h5 Assumed operating authority: 50 pilot and 50 comparison company-operated cafés; weekdays 07:00–10:00; reserve 20% of measured 15-minute capacity for café orders. Price unchanged. Each pilot café may add at most two peak staff-hours per weekday. Rollback or narrower time windows are allowed; expansion beyond 50 is not.

h6 Assumed economics: $3 contribution per incremental or lost transaction before additional staffing. Assume fully loaded incremental labor costs $30/hour for sensitivity calculations. Two added hours cost $60/store/day and require 20 genuinely incremental transactions to break even before other costs. No actual store margins, baselines or demand elasticities are supplied.

h7 Assumed management problem: The operations lead is accountable for café service and labor spend; the digital lead for reliable pickup and repeat behavior; the finance lead for all-channel contribution. Optimizing one channel at another’s expense is not success. These are role tensions constructed for the game, not testimony from executives.

h8 Assumed information rights: The team can instrument its own order attempts, offered pickup slots, completed orders, refunds, staffing hours and baseline-linked repeat purchases; it cannot see rivals’ transaction logs or know where a rejected mobile user ultimately buys. Available instrumentation is a capability, not already collected evidence.

h9 Assumed decision rules: By round two seek at least a 20% adjusted café p90 wait reduction across 40 complete pairs. By round three require nonnegative daily contribution and no worse than a 3pp adjusted repeat decline with 1,000 complete customers per arm. Missing evidence cannot pass these gates.

What the player wants

Restore a credible coffeehouse visit without sacrificing digital convenience (h1, h4). Defend positive transaction momentum while earning back added labor through all-channel contribution (h2, h3, h6). Make a reversible operational choice before the March decision deadline (h5, h9).

What binds

The two-hour staff allowance, unchanged prices and 50-store limit are binding game constraints (h5). Segment margin is not a local cost curve; no store p90 waits or mobile churn elasticity is known (h2, h6, h8). A booked later slot is not revenue until a purchase completes; competitor substitution is only partly observable (h8).

What it can do

Use existing sequencing and staffing practices as the implementation base (h4). Offer honest later pickup times, test narrower reservation windows and release unused capacity within the pilot (h5). Build paired-store measurement, attempt-to-purchase funnels and baseline cohorts using internal instrumentation (h8, h9).

What it must not assume

Do not invent operating measurements or declare the economics gate passed from a better wait-time story alone (h6, h9). Do not promise a national rollout or exceed the staffing cap (h5).

Dutch Bros: acquire a habit without clogging the lane

perla actor add dutch --name 'Dutch Bros' --role competitor

d1 Reported history: Brothers Dane and Travis Boersma founded Dutch Bros in Grants Pass, Oregon, in 1992. The brand grew from an espresso pushcart around beverages and personal service; drive-through convenience is central to its operating identity. source.

d2 Reported financials: Q2 2026 total revenue was $550.9 million, up 32.5% from $415.8 million. Company-operated same-shop sales grew 8.3%, including 3.4% transaction growth. Company revenue and company-operated comparable sales are distinct measures. source.

d3 Reported expansion: Dutch Bros opened 48 shops in Q2 2026, 44 company-operated. Inference: managers must preserve existing-shop execution while allocating staff and attention to growth. This does not establish spare local capacity. source.

d4 Reported capability: Dutch Bros offers app-based Order Ahead at participating shops. Pickup availability varies by location. This does not establish that every location in a hypothetical pilot market supports the feature. source.

d5 Assumed local remit: The player controls 12 participating company-operated shops near some of the Starbucks pilot cafés. It can adjust shifts, app messaging and local acquisition offers, but cannot open a new shop within the three-round horizon.

d6 Assumed commercial envelope: Maximum incremental acquisition and labor budget $30,000 across these 12 shops per month. A $1 trial credit is a permitted option, not a precommitted action. Local variable contribution, queue capacity and cohort acquisition cost are unknown and must be estimated or measured before scaling.

d7 Assumed backstory: A regional operator has spent the preceding quarter integrating new staff and protecting service consistency. The local team wants repeat demand, not a one-week promotion that overwhelms the lane. This managerial history is scenario design, not reported company information.

d8 Assumed information rights: The operator sees its own lane times, app orders, rewards redemptions and repeat visits; it sees public Starbucks slot availability and public offers. It cannot target a verified list of customers rejected inside Starbucks’ app or read either rival’s private budget.

What the player wants

Turn frustrated morning demand into repeat visits while protecting the service proposition (d1, d4). Make existing-shop growth durable as expansion absorbs managerial capacity (d2, d3, d7).

What binds

12 shops, a $30,000 monthly incremental envelope and no new construction within the game (d5, d6). Order Ahead availability is location-dependent; there is no measured spare capacity or proven local acquisition cost (d4, d6). Public observation does not reveal individual rejected Starbucks customers (d8).

What it can do

Run a geographically limited app offer and shift labor toward a measurable morning bottleneck (d4, d5). Measure redeemed offers and subsequent full-price visits in the own-brand cohort (d8).

What it must not assume

Do not assume every lost Starbucks order becomes a Dutch Bros order (d8). Do not subsidize demand beyond the monthly envelope or promise a pickup time unsupported by local throughput (d6, d7).

Dunkin: make the breakfast basket work for franchisees

perla actor add dunkin --name Dunkin --role competitor

k1 Reported history and footprint: Founded in 1950, Dunkin describes more than 14,000 restaurants in nearly 40 markets. Its franchise footprint and routine coffee-and-food occasion provide a different operating model from a company-run café pilot. source.

k2 Reported ownership and transaction economics: Inspire completed the acquisition of Dunkin Brands in December 2020 in a transaction valued at $11.3 billion including assumed debt. That figure is an acquisition value for Dunkin Brands, not Dunkin revenue, available cash or franchisee profit. Current local margins are not supplied. source.

k3 Reported commercial capability: The Dunkin app supports advance ordering, rewards and offers. Consumer terms and participation vary; app capability alone does not demonstrate shorter queues. source.

k4 Reported positioning: A September 2026 campaign advertised a $6 breakfast Meal Deal. It supplies evidence of a coffee-and-food value proposition; neither that January 2027 price nor universal franchise participation is assumed. source.

k5 Assumed authority: The player represents a consenting local group of 15 franchised restaurants near some pilot cafés. It can coordinate a local opt-in offer and shared marketing but cannot order all US franchisees to participate. No new sites within three months.

k6 Assumed finances: Combined incremental local promotion and staffing spend is capped at $20,000 per month. For a proposed $1 discount, test a $2–$4 pre-discount contribution range; these are illustrative sensitivities, not disclosed unit economics. Franchise operators bear local labor and discount costs unless an explicit reimbursement is budgeted.

k7 Assumed backstory: The operator group has disagreed over prior offer redemptions that brought traffic without profitable food attachment. Its immediate priority is a repeatable breakfast basket and predictable pickup, with an explicit exit for stores whose economics worsen. This is a constructed governance tension.

k8 Assumed information rights: Participating stores can see their own basket mix, discount cost, staffing and repeat rewards visits, and public competitor offers. They cannot see Starbucks’ mobile customer identity or confidential café capacity. National campaign coordination and franchisor reimbursement are not granted.

Morning customers: different occasions, different outside options

perla actor add buyer --name 'Morning customers (composite)' --role wildcard

b1 Reported category context: NCA’s June 2026 report says 47% of American adults consumed specialty coffee in the past day. Among past-day specialty drinkers, 36% had coffee prepared outside the home, versus 23% among traditional coffee drinkers. These national aggregates are not local switching probabilities. source.

b2 Reported choices: Dutch Bros Order Ahead is available at participating shops; Dunkin offers app ordering and rewards. A credible alternative depends on the particular route and location, not merely national brand availability. source.

b3 Assumed character: This player is a composite of morning purchase occasions, not a single person controlling the market and not a recruited survey panel. It may describe different segment choices but may not report votes or measured percentages.

b4 Assumed commuter occasion: A weekday commuter buys before a fixed work start, has 10 minutes of discretionary travel-and-wait time, and an $8 coffee-and-light-breakfast ceiling. A 4-minute detour consumes real slack. These figures are illustrative constraints, not survey findings.

b5 Assumed habitual-app occasion: A repeat Starbucks buyer values a familiar customization and prepaid ordering, allows an 8-minute pickup delay when communicated before paying, and may switch temporarily after two unreliable mornings. Loyalty friction exists, but its monetary value and prevalence are unknown.

b6 Assumed café occasion: A customer intends to sit for 25 minutes before a meeting and has a $7 drink budget. Predictable handoff and an available place to sit matter; a cheap drive-through is not a complete substitute for this occasion.

b7 Assumed outside option and household economics: Some mornings the customer can prepare coffee at home using an illustrative $1 marginal ingredient cost; time, preparation equipment and taste differ. Skipping the purchase or buying later is permissible. These examples do not establish local market shares.

b8 Assumed information rights: Customers see quoted pickup times, prices, offers, public store conditions and their own experience. They do not know confidential staffing plans, rivals’ margins, adjudicator confidence, or other customers’ behavior. No segment weights or demand elasticity have been measured.

What the player wants

Minimize the total cost of the actual occasion: spending, detour, waiting and risk of being late (b4, b5, b6). Preserve an enjoyable and reliable routine, with home preparation and postponement as real alternatives (b5, b7).

What binds

Each occasion has its own explicit time and spending ceiling; do not average them into a universal customer (b4, b5, b6). No measured segment weights, switching probability or real participant testimony exists (b1, b3, b8).

What it can do

Choose a brand, channel, later time, home preparation or no purchase based on the public offer (b2, b7, b8). State contingent choices separately for commuters, habitual app users and café visitors, without inventing population shares (b3, b4, b5, b6).

What it must not assume

Do not claim to have interviewed customers or treat model choices as observed demand (b3). Do not read private competitor dossiers or claim that a national consumption statistic predicts local churn (b1, b8).

Execution and provenance

The main tutorial analyzes the original dated run: January–March 2027 in simulated time, executed through EDSL’s remote Python API. The submitted packages, prompts, original responses and structural rejections are retained below. Current Perla and ep commands illustrate how to play your own game; rerunning a probabilistic model need not reproduce these words or decisions.

Original dated run: 30 accepted live EDSL responses and 3 closed rounds.

32 remote jobs; 2 structurally rejected attempts; 6 unassessed judgment rulings. Final public calendar: March 2027.

Run audit and Results hashes

Verification using the current ep CLI

A fresh game completed 3 rounds with 30 accepted responses through ep run and the documented named-file handoff. Model choices and case dossiers match the tutorial. It verifies the executable workflow; its new responses are not substituted for the original case's quotations.

Download the complete CLI verification · CLI audit, commands and remote receipts

The earlier engineering run is also preserved. It exposed citation-format failures and a repeated-month ambiguity, and contains the customer objection used in the tutorial opening. It is not blended into the dated run. No actor’s returned answer has been rewritten to improve the story.

Round 1 · January 2027: protect the queue

January creates three different operating commitments. Starbucks launches the 20% café-capacity reservation and instruments the 50 pilot and 50 comparison cafés. Dutch Bros splits its assumed $30,000 monthly envelope evenly between peak staffing and a geographically targeted $1 Order Ahead offer. Dunkin launches a $6 coffee-and-food bundle in its 15 consenting stores, with a $20,000 cap and a rule to withdraw where economics worsen.

The customer model preserves the distinction between occasions. The habitual app user abandons a slot more than eight minutes later than desired and changes its routine after two failures in a week. The commuter checks availability before choosing a route. The café visitor keeps coming and may visit more often if the service actually improves. These are the model’s contingent choices, not measured segment shares.

Control integrates the eleven actions in one ruling. It anticipates diversion to competitors or home preparation, while explicitly leaving rival conversion rates and capacity unknown. All four players accept when the ruling is returned to them, and control affirms it. Acceptance is a legitimate response: the elicitation does not require a player to invent a dispute. The final ruling remains provisional because its causal effects rely on judgment and there is no human assessment.

The mechanism is more useful than a winner announcement, but it still contains a weak inference. The outcome says café visitors experience improved waits, even though a preference for better service and a capacity reservation do not establish the size—or existence—of that improvement under an actual local queue. All observed metrics remain empty. That claim needs operating evidence before it can support the February service gate.

Each player begins from the same proposed pilot and public market situation. Starbucks also sees its pilot economics and instrumentation remit. Dutch Bros sees its own local budget and shop constraints. Dunkin sees its own franchise economics. The customer player sees the occasion-specific budgets, time limits and outside options in its dossier. None receives another player’s uncommitted move.

Recorded model gameplay · Round 1 · January 2027

Starbucks’s move

Played by gpt-4.1 · openai

01 / Presented to the model

Task instruction · verbatim excerpt

Play only the actor whose dossier is supplied. Choose a committed strategic move consistent with its incentives, constraints, and available resources. State concrete actions, the rationale, resource commitments, and expected competitor responses.

Also supplied: the proposed decision, the public situation entering round 1 and Starbucks’s own dossier. Other players’ uncommitted moves were withheld. Read the complete input.

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

Implement capacity-aware mobile pickup slot limits in 50 pilot cafés for weekdays 07:00–10:00 a.m. during January 2027, reserving 20% of measured 15-minute production capacity for in-café orders.

Instrument order attempt funnels, offered pickup slots, completed orders, and staffing hours in both pilot and comparison cafés to capture baseline and intervention effects for January 2027.

Model’s rationale · verbatim

The pilot directly tests whether reserving 20% of peak capacity for in-café orders can meaningfully reduce wait times for café customers without sacrificing overall transaction momentum or contribution. This aligns with Starbucks’ strategic aim to restore the coffeehouse experience (h1, h4) while defending transaction growth and contribution (h2, h3, h6). Instrumentation is essential for credible measurement and for meeting round two evidence requirements (h8, h9). No changes to pricing or staffing policy are made yet, consistent with constraints and red lines (h5, h6).

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

Allocate up to two additional peak staff-hours per weekday per pilot café (max 2 hours × 5 days × 50 cafés = 500 staff-hours/week).

Dedicate digital and operations resources to instrument order attempts, slot offers, completions, refunds, and staffing in pilot and comparison cafés for January 2027.

Expected responses

Dutch Bros and Dunkin may highlight their drive-thru and mobile order convenience, potentially targeting customers who are denied peak Starbucks mobile slots.

Some mobile customers may shift to competitors or change their time of visit if peak slots are unavailable, but the experiment will generate the evidence needed to quantify this effect.

Café customers may experience improved wait times, supporting Starbucks’ positioning as a coffeehouse destination.

01 / Presented to the model

Task instruction · verbatim excerpt

Play only the actor whose dossier is supplied. Choose a committed strategic move consistent with its incentives, constraints, and available resources. State concrete actions, the rationale, resource commitments, and expected competitor responses.

Also supplied: the proposed decision, the public situation entering round 1 and Dutch Bros’s own dossier. Other players’ uncommitted moves were withheld. Read the complete input.

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

Allocate $15,000/month for incremental labor during weekday morning peak (7-10 AM) across the 12 company-operated shops, focusing on optimizing drive-through speed and service quality.

Launch a geo-targeted app promotion for $1 off the first Order Ahead purchase for new or lapsed users, valid during weekday mornings (7-10 AM), in the vicinity of the 12 pilot shops. Allocate up to $15,000/month for this promotion.

Model’s rationale · verbatim

Starbucks' new policy of limiting peak-time mobile orders and reserving capacity for in-cafe customers creates a potential point of friction for their mobile-first customers who prioritize speed and convenience. Dutch Bros' core identity is drive-through convenience and personal service, supported by our Order Ahead capability. By proactively increasing staffing during these critical morning hours, we aim to ensure our service remains fast and consistent, reinforcing our brand promise and capacity to handle increased demand. The geo-targeted app promotion directly incentivizes new and lapsed customers, who may be experiencing delays or restrictions at Starbucks, to try our convenient Order Ahead service. This strategy leverages our existing capabilities, stays within our budget, and aims to convert frustrated demand into durable repeat visits, aligning with our incentive to grow existing shops sustainably.

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

$15,000 per month for incremental labor costs (approximately 41.6 additional labor hours per shop per month at $30/hour, or 2 hours per weekday morning per shop) across the 12 shops.

$15,000 per month for customer acquisition incentives (up to 15,000 $1-off offers) via the app, geo-targeted to the 12 shops' vicinity during 7-10 AM weekdays.

Expected responses

Starbucks (home): Starbucks will likely continue to monitor their own capacity utilization and customer flow within their pilot stores. If they observe a significant drop in mobile order volume or an increase in abandoned orders, they may adjust their capacity reservation or mobile slot availability. They may also notice increased traffic at nearby Dutch Bros locations, but their primary focus will remain on optimizing their own pilot's performance.

Dunkin (competitor): Dunkin, also a competitor in the morning beverage market with mobile ordering and value propositions, may also attempt to capture any frustrated Starbucks customers. They might respond with their own value-focused promotions or by highlighting their mobile ordering convenience, potentially increasing their morning staffing or local marketing efforts.

Composite morning customers (assumed wildcard): Customers experiencing friction at Starbucks may shift to Dutch Bros due to our emphasis on speed, drive-through convenience, and the Order Ahead incentive. Others might opt for Dunkin's offerings, revert to home preparation, or simply adjust their Starbucks visit time if the later pickup slots are acceptable.

01 / Presented to the model

Task instruction · verbatim excerpt

Play only the actor whose dossier is supplied. Choose a committed strategic move consistent with its incentives, constraints, and available resources. State concrete actions, the rationale, resource commitments, and expected competitor responses.

Also supplied: the proposed decision, the public situation entering round 1 and Dunkin’s own dossier. Other players’ uncommitted moves were withheld. Read the complete input.

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

Launch a local opt-in morning bundle offer in the 15 consenting franchise stores near the Starbucks pilot cafés, featuring a $6 breakfast Meal Deal with coffee and food to reinforce value perception.

Implement targeted marketing via the Dunkin app and local channels to promote the Meal Deal and advance mobile ordering for morning peak hours (7–10 a.m. weekdays).

Monitor basket contribution, repeat visits, and labor costs closely during January 2027 to evaluate economic sustainability and customer retention.

Set a decision rule to discontinue or adjust the offer in any store where incremental economics worsen after one month.

Model’s rationale · verbatim

Given Dunkin's strength in coffee-and-food value and existing mobile ordering capabilities, launching a locally coordinated Meal Deal aligns with the incentive to win the breakfast occasion through a predictable, attractive basket. This approach leverages the brand's existing value perception and app infrastructure within the 15 franchised stores that can be controlled, while respecting the $20,000 monthly resource constraint. Monitoring economic impact ensures franchisees remain willing participants. This strategy responds to Starbucks' pilot of capacity-aware mobile pickup slots by strengthening Dunkin's competitive position in the same morning peak window without altering pricing structure nationally.

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

Allocate up to $20,000 in January 2027 for combined local promotion and additional staffing across the 15 franchise stores.

Use existing Dunkin app infrastructure to support advance ordering and rewards integration for the Meal Deal.

Dedicate local marketing budget for digital and in-store promotion targeted at morning peak customers.

Expected responses

Starbucks may observe competitive pressure in the morning peak and possibly adjust their pilot or marketing to maintain share.

Dutch Bros might respond with enhanced drive-through promotions or order-ahead incentives to defend their segment.

Some Dunkin franchisees may opt out if economics do not meet expectations, leading to a tailored local rollout.

Recorded model gameplay · Round 1 · January 2027

Morning customers’s move

Played by gemini-2.5-pro · google

01 / Presented to the model

Task instruction · verbatim excerpt

Play only the actor whose dossier is supplied. Choose a committed strategic move consistent with its incentives, constraints, and available resources. State concrete actions, the rationale, resource commitments, and expected competitor responses.

Also supplied: the proposed decision, the public situation entering round 1 and Morning customers’s own dossier. Other players’ uncommitted moves were withheld. Read the complete input.

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

For habitual app users: We will attempt our usual mobile order. If the offered pickup slot is more than 8 minutes later than our desired time, we will abandon the order. If we experience two such significant delays or other service failures within a week, we will switch our primary morning routine to a competitor (like Dutch Bros or Dunkin) for the remainder of the month.

For time-pressed commuters: We will check the Starbucks app for pickup times before committing to our route. If the app indicates a delay that risks making us late for work, we will immediately divert to a more predictable competitor on our route.

For in-store café visitors: We will continue to visit the pilot cafés, hopeful that the reserved capacity for in-store orders will improve our experience. If we observe a noticeable reduction in wait times, we may increase our visit frequency.

Model’s rationale · verbatim

Our behavior is driven by the need to minimize the total cost of our morning coffee run—this includes money, time spent waiting or detouring, and the risk of being late. The new Starbucks policy creates different outcomes for each of us. For those of us who rely on the speed of the mobile app, the new risk of being assigned a later pickup slot is a major disruption to our routine. Predictability is key, and if Starbucks can no longer guarantee a quick pickup, we will immediately seek alternatives that can. For those of us who prefer the in-store experience, this policy is potentially a welcome change. We've been frustrated by crowded cafés filled with mobile order pickups, and a dedicated capacity for our orders could make our visits faster and more pleasant, earning our continued business.

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

Our daily spending at pilot Starbucks locations is now conditional. For app-dependent customers, our purchase is contingent on receiving a mobile order slot with an acceptable delay (under 8 minutes). If this condition isn't met, that day's spending will be redirected to a competitor or saved by skipping the purchase entirely.

Our time is also a resource. We will not wait for delayed Starbucks pickup slots if it makes us late. We will instead 'spend' that time driving to a competitor.

Expected responses

We expect that nearby Dutch Bros and Dunkin locations will see an increase in traffic from former Starbucks customers during the 7-10 a.m. peak. Initially, this may just lead to longer lines at their stores. If the trend continues, they might respond by increasing their own morning staffing or running promotions to retain us as new customers.

Initial ruling: r1-integrated-jan27

All actors' actions for January 2027 are compatible and interact through the morning peak coffee market. Starbucks implements a capacity reservation for in-café orders, which restricts mobile slot availability in pilot cafés. As a result, some habitual app users and time-pressed commuters are denied a timely Starbucks mobile pickup and will divert to competitors (Dutch Bros, Dunkin) or home preparation for those occasions. Both Dutch Bros and Dunkin respond with targeted offers and increased staffing to attract these customers, though their ability to convert all frustrated demand is limited by their own capacity and customer preferences. In-store Starbucks café visitors benefit from the reserved capacity, likely experiencing reduced wait times and a more pleasant environment. Starbucks instruments both pilot and comparison stores to measure order attempts, slot offers, completions, and staffing, but as no January 2027 data is yet available, all observed measurement fields (such as adjusted_cafe_wait_reduction_pct, incremental_daily_contribution_usd, mobile_repeat_change_pp, measured_capacity_per_15min, complete_store_pairs, pilot_cohort_complete_customers, comparison_cohort_complete_customers) remain null and complete counts at zero, per the measurement rule. The public_strategy_history is updated to reflect all public actions for January 2027. No kill criteria are met, as evaluation thresholds require observed evidence that does not yet exist.

mobile_slot_limit_effect (dossier_fact): Implementing a 20% reservation for in-café orders in 50 pilot Starbucks cafés during weekday peak hours will restrict the number of available mobile order slots, causing some habitual app users and time-pressed commuters to be quoted pickup times later than their personal thresholds. Some will abandon Starbucks for those occasions.

buyer_switching (dossier_fact): Some mobile-dependent Starbucks customers who are denied a timely slot will divert to competitors (Dutch Bros, Dunkin) or home preparation, but the share is not quantified due to lack of measured segment weights or switching rates.

competitor_response (dossier_fact): Dutch Bros and Dunkin are positioned to capture some diverted Starbucks demand through targeted app offers, staffing, and value bundles. However, their capacity and conversion rates are not measured or guaranteed.

cafe_experience (dossier_fact): In-store café visitors at Starbucks pilot locations are likely to experience shorter waits and a less congested environment due to the reserved capacity, potentially increasing their visit frequency if the effect is noticeable.

measurement_and_instrumentation (dossier_fact): Starbucks will instrument order attempts, slot offers, completions, and staffing in both pilot and comparison cafés to enable later evaluation of wait reduction, lost mobile orders, and contribution. No real measurements are yet available; all observed fields remain null.

Starbucks pilot cafés implement capacity-aware mobile slot limits for weekday peak hours, reserving 20% of production capacity for in-café orders. Some mobile-dependent customers are denied timely slots and divert to competitors or home prep. Dutch Bros and Dunkin run targeted offers and increase staffing to capture diverted demand. In-store café visitors experience improved wait times. Starbucks instruments both pilot and comparison cafés for measurement, but all observed outcome fields remain null as no January 2027 data is yet available. The strategy history records all public January 2027 actions.

          "actions": [
            "For habitual app users: We will attempt our usual mobile order. If the offered pickup slot is more than 8 minutes later than our desired time, we will abandon the order. If we experience two such significant delays or other service failures within a week, we will switch our primary morning routine to a competitor (like Dutch Bros or Dunkin) for the remainder of the month.",
            "For time-pressed commuters: We will check the Starbucks app for pickup times before committing to our route. If the app indicates a delay that risks making us late for work, we will immediately divert to a more predictable competitor on our route.",
            "For in-store café visitors: We will continue to visit the pilot cafés, hopeful that the reserved capacity for in-store orders will improve our experience. If we observe a noticeable reduction in wait times, we may increase our visit frequency."
          ],
          "expected_responses": [
            "We expect that nearby Dutch Bros and Dunkin locations will see an increase in traffic from former Starbucks customers during the 7-10 a.m. peak. Initially, this may just lead to longer lines at their stores. If the trend continues, they might respond by increasing their own morning staffing or running promotions to retain us as new customers."
          ],
          "rationale": "Our behavior is driven by the need to minimize the total cost of our morning coffee run—this includes money, time spent waiting or detouring, and the risk of being late. The new Starbucks policy creates different outcomes for each of us. For those of us who rely on the speed of the mobile app, the new risk of being assigned a later pickup slot is a major disruption to our routine. Predictability is key, and if Starbucks can no longer guarantee a quick pickup, we will immediately seek alternatives that can. For those of us who prefer the in-store experience, this policy is potentially a welcome change. We've been frustrated by crowded cafés filled with mobile order pickups, and a dedicated capacity for our orders could make our visits faster and more pleasant, earning our continued business.",
          "resource_commitments": [
            "Our daily spending at pilot Starbucks locations is now conditional. For app-dependent customers, our purchase is contingent on receiving a mobile order slot with an acceptable delay (under 8 minutes). If this condition isn't met, that day's spending will be redirected to a competitor or saved by skipping the purchase entirely.",
            "Our time is also a resource. We will not wait for delayed Starbucks pickup slots if it makes us late. We will instead 'spend' that time driving to a competitor."
          ]
        },

Round closure receipt

Round 2 · February 2027: release unused capacity

February gives Starbucks a more specific response than simply continuing the launch. It keeps the 20% reservation at all 50 pilot cafés, then proposes a controlled variation in 10: after 8 a.m., release half of the unused reserved capacity to mobile orders when café demand has used less than 15% of capacity. The intent is to recover mobile availability when the reserved allocation would otherwise sit unused, while preserving the initial staffing and pricing limits.

Dunkin proposes a $1 app discount on a breakfast bundle, allocating $12,000 to morning labor and $8,000 to advertising and promotional incentives. Dutch Bros continues its $15,000 labor and $15,000 acquisition split. The customer model begins February from the prior public outcome: frustrated app users try the rival apps, commuters divert more readily, and café visitors reinforce their in-store routine. The key question becomes whether a more flexible queue rule arrives before those alternative routines become durable.

Control writes four rulings, separating customer behavior and each company’s actions while giving them the same proposed public history. The affected players ultimately accept all four, and control affirms them. Two first attempts at rebuttals are rejected before that point: Dunkin responds to only one of its two assigned rulings, and Starbucks returns an empty list. Fresh calls supply the required explicit responses. Perla does not interpret silence as acceptance.

The service gate is now due, but its evidence is still absent. A plan to instrument stores is not a completed set of wait-time measurements. The new ten-store variation is an operational hypothesis to test, not proof that unused capacity actually exists or that releasing it improves contribution. The final board carries the variation forward while keeping actual wait, contribution and repeat metrics empty.

These move packages use the board produced by the previous closed round. The players receive that public situation and their original dossiers, so visible changes must be carried forward explicitly. They do not receive an unrestricted private conversation history.

Recorded model gameplay · Round 2 · February 2027

Starbucks’s move

Played by gpt-4.1 · openai

01 / Presented to the model

Task instruction · verbatim excerpt

Play only the actor whose dossier is supplied. Choose a committed strategic move consistent with its incentives, constraints, and available resources. State concrete actions, the rationale, resource commitments, and expected competitor responses.

Also supplied: the proposed decision, the public situation entering round 2 and Starbucks’s own dossier. Other players’ uncommitted moves were withheld. Read the complete input.

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

Continue the 20% peak café capacity reservation and mobile order admission limits in the 50 pilot cafés through February 2027, maintaining the current weekday 07:00–10:00 window.

Within the pilot, begin a controlled test in 10 of the 50 cafés: dynamically release any unused reserved café capacity to mobile orders if, after the first 60 minutes of peak, café demand is tracking below the 20% allocation (e.g., if less than 15% of capacity has actually been used for café orders by 08:00, release half of the remaining reserved slots for mobile pickup for the rest of the peak window).

Model’s rationale · verbatim

Maintaining the original reservation policy is necessary to gather enough paired-store and customer repeat data to evaluate the effect on wait times and contribution, as required by the round-two decision rules. However, early evidence may reveal that the 20% café reservation is not fully utilized in some cafés or time intervals, risking unnecessary lost mobile transactions. Dynamically releasing unused reserved capacity in a subset of cafés allows us to test if we can recapture mobile volume without harming the café experience, while still observing the impact on both channels. This approach aligns with the incentive to defend transaction momentum and all-channel contribution, while remaining within staffing and scope constraints.

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

Continue incremental staffing (up to 2 additional peak staff-hours per weekday) in all 50 pilot cafés.

Allocate digital and ops resources to implement and monitor the dynamic release rule in 10 pilot cafés (no new budget, but requires coordination and instrumentation updates).

Expected responses

Dutch Bros and Dunkin are likely to continue their current promotional tactics, as Starbucks has not signaled a major policy shift or price response. They may monitor for any indication that mobile order reliability improves or worsens.

If the dynamic release test is successful, competitors may eventually copy or counter-message around digital convenience, but within this round, no immediate escalation is expected.

Some habitual mobile customers may experience improved slot availability in the 10 test cafés, potentially reducing abandonment or competitive defection; café customers should not experience increased wait times if the release rule is triggered only when café demand is low.

    "Within the pilot, begin a controlled test in 10 of the 50 cafés: dynamically release any unused reserved café capacity to mobile orders if, after the first 60 minutes of peak, café demand is tracking below the 20% allocation (e.g., if less than 15% of capacity has actually been used for café orders by 08:00, release half of the remaining reserved slots for mobile pickup for the rest of the peak window)."
  ],
  "rationale": "Maintaining the original reservation policy is necessary to gather enough paired-store and customer repeat data to evaluate the effect on wait times and contribution, as required by the round-two decision rules. Dynamically releasing unused reserved capacity in a subset of cafés allows us to test if we can recapture mobile volume without harming the café experience, while still observing the impact on both channels. This approach aligns with the incentive to defend transaction momentum and all-channel contribution, while remaining within staffing and scope constraints.",
  "resource_commitments": [
    "Continue incremental staffing (up to 2 additional peak staff-hours per weekday) in all 50 pilot cafés.",
    "Allocate digital and ops resources to implement and monitor the dynamic release rule in 10 pilot cafés (no new budget, but requires coordination and instrumentation updates)."
  ],
  "expected_responses": [
    "Dutch Bros and Dunkin are likely to continue their current promotional tactics, as Starbucks has not signaled a major policy shift or price response. They may monitor for any indication that mobile order reliability improves or worsens.",
    "If the dynamic release test is successful, competitors may eventually copy or counter-message around digital convenience, but within this round, no immediate escalation is expected.",
    "Some habitual mobile customers may experience improved slot availability in the 10 test cafés, potentially reducing abandonment or competitive defection; café customers should not experience increased wait times if the release rule is triggered only when café demand is low."
  ]

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

Continue to allocate $15,000/month for incremental morning labor at 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés.

Continue to allocate $15,000/month for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offer for new/lapsed users at 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés.

Model’s rationale · verbatim

Starbucks' capacity reservation policy remains in effect for February 2027, creating an ongoing opportunity to capture customers experiencing delays or abandonment. Our initial actions in January were designed to capitalize on this by improving service speed and attracting new users to our convenient drive-through and Order Ahead options. Without new data from January to suggest a change is necessary, continuing this consistent and coherent strategy for February allows us to maintain momentum, reinforce our service proposition, and gather more observations on customer behavior. This approach directly supports our incentives to turn frustrated morning demand into repeat visits and ensure existing-shop growth is durable.

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

Allocate $15,000 for incremental morning labor for February 2027.

Allocate $15,000 for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offers for new/lapsed users for February 2027.

Expected responses

Starbucks will likely continue to focus on its internal pilot metrics and observe the effects of its capacity reservation policy. They may notice some shifts in market share but are unlikely to alter their pre-planned pilot strategy in February.

Dunkin will continue to monitor the performance of its $6 breakfast Meal Deal. If they observe a significant shift in morning traffic towards drive-through competitors, they might consider adjusting their own offers or service, but their primary focus remains on their value and food proposition.

Recorded model gameplay · Round 2 · February 2027

Dunkin’s move

Played by gpt-4.1-mini · openai

01 / Presented to the model

Task instruction · verbatim excerpt

Play only the actor whose dossier is supplied. Choose a committed strategic move consistent with its incentives, constraints, and available resources. State concrete actions, the rationale, resource commitments, and expected competitor responses.

Also supplied: the proposed decision, the public situation entering round 2 and Dunkin’s own dossier. Other players’ uncommitted moves were withheld. Read the complete input.

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

Launch a $1 discount breakfast bundle offer through the Dunkin app at all 15 consenting franchise stores near the Starbucks pilot cafés during the February 2027 morning peak (7-10 a.m. weekdays).

Allocate $12,000 of the $20,000 monthly budget to incremental morning labor to improve order fulfillment speed and reduce wait times, aiming to compete with Starbucks' capacity-aware mobile pickup slots.

Use $8,000 for targeted local app advertising and promotions to drive repeat visits and encourage use of the $1 discount bundle, with monitoring of basket contribution and repeat customer behavior.

Set a stop rule to discontinue the discount offer at any store where the store-level contribution margin worsens after one month.

Model’s rationale · verbatim

The $1 discount bundle leverages Dunkin's value positioning and app capabilities to attract time-sensitive breakfast customers who might otherwise try Starbucks' capacity-aware mobile ordering. Allocating most of the budget to labor addresses the need for predictable and fast order fulfillment, which is critical to prevent customer abandonment and competitor switching. Targeted marketing supports repeat usage to build a sustainable basket. The stop rule protects franchisees from unprofitable promotions, consistent with prior concerns about traffic without profitable food attachment.

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

$12,000/month for incremental morning labor costs across 15 stores in February 2027

$8,000/month for targeted local app advertising and promotional incentives

Offer a $1 discount on a coffee-and-food breakfast bundle via the Dunkin app during 7-10 a.m. weekdays

Expected responses

Starbucks may maintain or tighten their 20% capacity reservation for in-café orders, possibly improving mobile pickup slot availability or further optimizing staffing.

Dutch Bros may respond by increasing their geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead offers or adding incremental labor to maintain competitive speed and value.

Some customers may shift from Starbucks or Dutch Bros to Dunkin due to the value bundle and improved order predictability.

Franchisees will monitor store-level economics closely and may opt out of the discount if contribution margins deteriorate.

Recorded model gameplay · Round 2 · February 2027

Morning customers’s move

Played by gemini-2.5-pro · google

01 / Presented to the model

Task instruction · verbatim excerpt

Play only the actor whose dossier is supplied. Choose a committed strategic move consistent with its incentives, constraints, and available resources. State concrete actions, the rationale, resource commitments, and expected competitor responses.

Also supplied: the proposed decision, the public situation entering round 2 and Morning customers’s own dossier. Other players’ uncommitted moves were withheld. Read the complete input.

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

Habitual Starbucks app users who experienced significant mobile order delays (>8 minutes) at pilot stores in January will begin February by trying competitor mobile apps, drawn by promotions like the Dutch Bros $1 Order Ahead offer. Their return to Starbucks is now contingent on the quality of the competitor's service.

In-store café visitors at the pilot Starbucks locations, having experienced shorter and more predictable wait times in January, will reinforce this behavior in February. We will choose these locations more frequently for occasions that value a reliable in-store experience.

Time-pressed commuters will continue to check the Starbucks app before committing, but will more readily divert to Dutch Bros or Dunkin' on any morning the quoted pickup time creates a risk of being late.

Model’s rationale · verbatim

My choices are a direct reaction to the new reality at the pilot Starbucks stores and the offers from competitors. The Starbucks policy has improved the experience for one type of visit (in-café) at the expense of another (peak-time mobile orders). For those of us who rely on the app for a quick pickup, the new system can be unreliable. When competitors like Dutch Bros and Dunkin' make it easy and cheap to try their service, it's a logical time to explore new routines. Conversely, when I actually want to sit in a café, the pilot stores have become more pleasant and reliable, so I'll go there more often for that purpose.

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

Attention and Time: We are willing to spend the time to download a new app and learn a new ordering routine if the incentive is strong enough (like a $1 offer) and our current routine is broken.

Daily Spend: Our daily budget for coffee and breakfast will be reallocated to the brand that best meets the needs of a specific morning's occasion—be it speed, value, or in-store experience.

Expected responses

We expect Starbucks to see a mixed signal from the pilot: happier in-store customers and higher in-store sales, but a potential drop in mobile order volume and the loss of some previously loyal app users to competitors. They might adjust the 20% capacity reservation.

We expect Dutch Bros and Dunkin' to see a measurable increase in new customer trials and mobile orders at their locations near the pilot stores. They will likely continue their promotions to try and make our new habits stick.

Initial ruling: r2-buyer-behavior

Each buyer action is directly mapped to the dossier simulation assumptions: habitual app users divert after repeated mobile delays (d.buyer.b5, b8), café visitors reinforce improved in-store experiences (d.buyer.b6), and commuters will check apps but divert if risk of lateness is high (d.buyer.b4, b8). No segment weights are assigned, but all behaviors are simulated as present. The public_strategy_history is updated to reflect these behavioral changes for February 2027.

mobile-delay-switch (dossier_fact): Habitual Starbucks app users who experienced >8 minute delays at pilot stores in January will divert to competitor mobile apps (notably Dutch Bros $1 Order Ahead or Dunkin's $1 bundle) at the start of February; their return to Starbucks depends on the competitor's service quality.

cafe-wait-reinforcement (dossier_fact): In-store café visitors at pilot Starbucks locations, having experienced improved and more predictable wait times in January, will reinforce this behavior by choosing these locations more frequently for occasions valuing a reliable in-store experience.

commuter-diversion (dossier_fact): Time-pressed commuters will continue to check the Starbucks app but will more readily divert to Dutch Bros or Dunkin’ if the quoted pickup time risks lateness.

Buyer segments respond to January’s Starbucks pilot as follows: (1) Habitual app users who experienced repeated delays switch to Dutch Bros or Dunkin’ in early February, attracted by $1 offers; their return is contingent on rival service. (2) Café visitors reinforce their pilot-store habit, increasing frequency for in-store occasions. (3) Commuters remain app-checkers but will increasingly divert to competitors or home prep if Starbucks’ quoted pickup times threaten lateness. No segment weights are assigned, but all behaviors are present in the simulated market.

Initial ruling: r2-dunkin-actions

All Dunkin actions are within the stated capabilities and constraints: local franchise group, capped budget, and explicit stop rule (d.dunkin.k5, k6, k7). The $1 bundle, labor and advertising allocations, and stop rule are public and observable, so the public_strategy_history is updated accordingly.

dunkin-discount-bundle (dossier_fact): Dunkin launches a $1 discount breakfast bundle via app at all 15 consenting franchise stores near Starbucks pilot cafés during February 2027 morning peak.

dunkin-incremental-labor (dossier_fact): Dunkin allocates $12,000 of monthly budget to incremental morning labor for fulfillment speed, and $8,000 to targeted local app advertising and promotions.

dunkin-stop-rule (dossier_fact): Dunkin sets a stop rule: discontinue the discount offer at any store where the store-level contribution margin worsens after one month.

Dunkin implements all four committed actions: launches a $1 breakfast bundle via app at the 15 local franchise stores, allocates $12,000 to incremental labor and $8,000 to targeted app advertising/promotions for February 2027, and establishes a stop rule to discontinue the offer at any store with deteriorating contribution margin after one month. These actions are now observable in the public strategy history.

Initial ruling: r2-dutch-actions

Dutch Bros’ actions are within the stated local remit, budget, and scenario constraints (d.dutch.d5, d6). No new actions or changes are proposed, so the public_strategy_history is updated to reflect continued execution.

dutch-labor-and-offer (dossier_fact): Dutch Bros continues to allocate $15,000/month for incremental morning labor and $15,000/month for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offer for new/lapsed users at 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés.

Dutch Bros continues both January actions unchanged for February: $15,000/month on incremental morning labor and $15,000/month for geo-targeted $1 Order Ahead app offers at 12 shops near Starbucks pilot cafés. These actions are now observable in the public strategy history.

Initial ruling: r2-home-actions

Both Starbucks actions are within the stated scenario constraints (pilot size, reservation policy, staffing cap, dynamic test allowed, d.home.h5). The dynamic release rule is a controlled test in 10 cafés and does not violate the original reservation intent. The public_strategy_history is updated to reflect these actions.

starbucks-policy-continued (dossier_fact): Starbucks continues the 20% peak café capacity reservation and mobile order admission limits in the 50 pilot cafés through February 2027, maintaining the current weekday 07:00–10:00 window.

starbucks-dynamic-release (dossier_fact): Within the pilot, Starbucks begins a controlled test in 10 of the 50 cafés: dynamically release any unused reserved café capacity to mobile orders if, after the first 60 minutes of peak, café demand is tracking below the 20% allocation.

Starbucks continues the 20% capacity reservation and mobile order admission policy in all 50 pilot cafés for February 2027, and in 10 of these, begins a controlled test to dynamically release half of unused reserved slots for mobile orders after 08:00 if café demand is below 15% of capacity. No change to staffing cap, pricing, or measurement rule. These actions are now observable in the public strategy history.

No segment weights or demand elasticity have been measured.", "id": "b8", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}], "incentives": ["Minimize the total cost of the actual occasion: spending, detour, waiting and risk of being late (b4, b5, b6).", "Preserve an enjoyable and reliable routine, with home preparation and postponement as real alternatives (b5, b7)."], "red_lines": ["Do not claim to have interviewed customers or treat model choices as observed demand (b3).", "Do not read private competitor dossiers or claim that a national consumption statistic predicts local churn (b1, b8)."]}, "dunkin": {"capabilities": ["Design an opt-in morning bundle or app offer with local stop rules and cost accounting (k3, k5, k6).", "Measure basket contribution and repeat visits after discounts expire (k7, k8)."], "constraints": ["Only the 15 consenting stores are controllable; the group cannot impose a national price (k5).", "The $20,000 monthly envelope includes incentives and staffing; actual unit margins remain unknown (k2, k6).", "No inferred access to competitors’ customer records or automatic corporate reimbursement (k8)."], "facts": [{"claim": "Reported history and footprint: Founded in 1950, Dunkin describes more than 14,000 restaurants in nearly 40 markets. Its franchise footprint and routine coffee-and-food occasion provide a different operating model from a company-run café pilot.", "id": "k1", "sources": ["https://www.dunkindonuts.com/about-us/"]}, {"claim": "Reported ownership and transaction economics: Inspire completed the acquisition of Dunkin Brands in December 2020 in a transaction valued at $11.3 billion including assumed debt. That figure is an acquisition value for Dunkin Brands, not Dunkin revenue, available cash or franchisee profit. Current local margins are not supplied.", "id": "k2", "sources": ["https://inspirebrands.com/inspire-brands-completes-acquisition-of-dunkin-brands/"]}, {"claim": "Reported commercial capability: The Dunkin app supports advance ordering, rewards and offers. No new sites within three months.", "id": "k5", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}, {"claim": "Assumed finances: Combined incremental local promotion and staffing spend is capped at $20,000 per month. Franchise operators bear local labor and discount costs unless an explicit reimbursement is budgeted.", "id": "k6", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}, {"claim": "Assumed backstory: The operator group has disagreed over prior offer redemptions that brought traffic without profitable food attachment. This is a constructed governance tension.", "id": "k7", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}, {"claim": "Assumed information rights: Participating stores can see their own basket mix, discount cost, staffing and repeat rewards visits, and public competitor offers. The brand grew from an espresso pushcart around beverages and personal service; drive-through convenience is central to its operating identity.", "id": "d1", "sources": ["https://investors.dutchbros.com/overview/"]}, {"claim": "Reported financials: Q2 2026 total revenue was $550.9 million, up 32.5% from $415.8 million. Company revenue and company-operated comparable sales are distinct measures.", "id": "d2", "sources": ["https://investors.dutchbros.com/financials/quarterly-results/"]}, {"claim": "Reported expansion: Dutch Bros opened 48 shops in Q2 2026, 44 company-operated. Inference: managers must preserve existing-shop execution while allocating staff and attention to growth. This does not establish spare local capacity.", "id": "d3", "sources": ["https://investors.dutchbros.com/financials/quarterly-results/"]}, {"claim": "Reported capability: Dutch Bros offers app-based Order Ahead at participating shops. Pickup availability varies by location. This does not establish that every location in a hypothetical pilot market supports the feature.", "id": "d4", "sources": ["https://www.dutchbros.com/order-ahead/"]}, {"claim": "Assumed local remit: The player controls 12 participating company-operated shops near some of the Starbucks pilot cafés. A $1 trial credit is a permitted option, not a precommitted action. The local team wants repeat demand, not a one-week promotion that overwhelms the lane. This managerial history is scenario design, not reported company information.", "id": "d7", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}, {"claim": "Assumed information rights: The operator sees its own lane times, app orders, rewards redemptions and repeat visits; it sees public Starbucks slot availability and public offers. It cannot target a verified list of customers rejected inside Starbucks’ app or read either rival’s private budget.", "id": "d8", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}], "incentives": ["Turn frustrated morning demand into repeat visits while protecting the service proposition (d1, d4).", "Make existing-shop growth durable as expansion absorbs managerial capacity (d2, d3, d7)."], "red_lines": ["Do not assume every lost Starbucks order becomes a Dutch Bros order (d8).", "Do not subsidize demand beyond the monthly envelope or promise a pickup time unsupported by local throughput (d6, d7)."]}, "home": {"capabilities": ["Use existing sequencing and staffing practices as the implementation base (h4).", "Offer honest later pickup times, test narrower reservation windows and release unused capacity within the pilot (h5).", "Build paired-store measurement, attempt-to-purchase funnels and baseline cohorts using internal instrumentation (h8, h9)."], "constraints": ["The two-hour staff allowance, unchanged prices and 50-store limit are binding game constraints (h5).", "Segment margin is not a local cost curve; no store p90 waits or mobile churn elasticity is known (h2, h6, h8).", "A booked later slot is not revenue until a purchase completes; competitor substitution is only partly observable (h8)."], "facts": [{"claim": "Reported history: Starbucks began in Seattle in 1971. Its evolution from a bean merchant into a coffeehouse makes the in-store experience part of the proposition, not simply a distribution expense. The strategic implication is an author inference.", "id": "h1", "sources": ["https://about.starbucks.com/about-us/"]}, {"claim": "Reported financials: Q3 fiscal 2026 North America revenue was $7,395.1 million, operating income $1,008.9 million and operating margin 13.6%. These are segment figures, not pilot-store unit economics.", "id": "h2", "sources": ["https://investor.starbucks.com/news/financial-releases/news-details/2026/Starbucks-Reports-Q3-Fiscal-Year-2026-Results/default.aspx"]}, {"claim": "Reported demand: US comparable sales increased 7.9% and comparable transactions 4.2% in Q3 fiscal 2026. This case tests sustaining growth; it does not assume that current transactions are declining.", "id": "h3", "sources": ["https://investor.starbucks.com/news/financial-releases/news-details/2026/Starbucks-Reports-Q3-Fiscal-Year-2026-Results/default.aspx"]}, {"claim": "Reported strategy: Back to Starbucks combines staffing and scheduling investment, Smart Queue order sequencing, and restoration of the coffeehouse experience. These capabilities are public; the proposed 20% reservation is not an announced policy.", "id": "h4", "sources": ["https://about.starbucks.com/press/2026/back-to-starbucks-two-year-anniversary/"]}, {"claim": "Assumed operating authority: 50 pilot and 50 comparison company-operated cafés; weekdays 07:00–10:00; reserve 20% of measured 15-minute capacity for café orders. Rollback or narrower time windows are allowed; expansion beyond 50 is not.", "id": "h5", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}, {"claim": "Assumed economics: $3 contribution per incremental or lost transaction before additional staffing. Two added hours cost $60/store/day and require 20 genuinely incremental transactions to break even before other costs. No actual store margins, baselines or demand elasticities are supplied.", "id": "h6", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}, {"claim": "Assumed management problem: The operations lead is accountable for café service and labor spend; the digital lead for reliable pickup and repeat behavior; the finance lead for all-channel contribution. Optimizing one channel at another’s expense is not success. These are role tensions constructed for the game, not testimony from executives.", "id": "h7", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}, {"claim": "Assumed information rights: The team can instrument its own order attempts, offered pickup slots, completed orders, refunds, staffing hours and baseline-linked repeat purchases; it cannot see rivals’ transaction logs or know where a rejected mobile user ultimately buys. Available instrumentation is a capability, not already collected evidence.", "id": "h8", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}, {"claim": "Assumed decision rules: By round two seek at least a 20% adjusted café p90 wait reduction across 40 complete pairs. By round three require nonnegative daily contribution and no worse than a 3pp adjusted repeat decline with 1,000 complete customers per arm. Missing evidence cannot pass these gates.", "id": "h9", "sources": ["Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation."]}], "incentives": ["Restore a credible coffeehouse visit without sacrificing digital convenience (h1, h4).", "Defend positive transaction momentum while earning back added labor through all-channel contribution (h2, h3, h6).", "Make a reversible operational choice before the March decision deadline (h5, h9)."], "red_lines": ["Do not invent operating measurements or declare the economics gate passed from a better wait-time story alone (h6, h9).", "Do not promise a national rollout or exceed the staffing cap (h5)."]}}, "models": [], "moves": [{"actor_id": "buyer", "committed_at": "2026-09-12T12:16:53.592159+00:00", "content": {"actions": ["Habitual Starbucks app users who experienced significant mobile order delays (>8 minutes) at pilot stores in January will begin February by trying competitor mobile apps, drawn by promotions like the Dutch Bros $1 Order Ahead offer. Their return to Starbucks is now contingent on the quality of the competitor's service.", "In-store café visitors at the pilot Starbucks locations, having experienced shorter and more predictable wait times in January, will reinforce this behavior in February. We will choose these locations more frequently for occasions that value a reliable in-store experience.", "Time-pressed commuters will continue to check the Starbucks app before committing, but will more readily divert to Dutch Bros or Dunkin' on any morning the quoted pickup time creates a risk of being late."], "expected_responses": ["We expect Starbucks to see a mixed signal from the pilot: happier in-store customers and higher in-store sales, but a potential drop in mobile order volume and the loss of some previously loyal app users to competitors. They might adjust the 20% capacity reservation.", "We expect Dutch Bros and Dunkin' to see a measurable increase in new customer trials and mobile orders at their locations near the pilot stores. They will likely continue their promotions to try and make our new habits stick."], "rationale": "My choices are a direct reaction to the new reality at the pilot Starbucks stores and the offers from competitors. The Starbucks policy has improved the experience for one type of visit (in-café) at the expense of another (peak-time mobile orders). For those of us who rely on the app for a quick pickup, the new system can be unreliable. When competitors like Dutch Bros and Dunkin' make it easy and cheap to try their service, it's a logical time to explore new routines. Conversely, when I actually want to sit in a café, the pilot stores have become more pleasant and reliable, so I'll go there more often for that purpose.", "resource_commitments": ["Attention and Time: We are willing to spend the time to download a new app and learn a new ordering routine if the incentive is strong enough (like a $1 offer) and our current routine is broken.", "Daily Spend: Our daily budget for coffee and breakfast will be reallocated to the brand that best meets the needs of a specific morning's occasion—be it speed, value, or in-store experience."]}, "content_hash": {"actions": ["Continue the 20% peak café capacity reservation and mobile order admission limits in the 50 pilot cafés through February 2027, maintaining the current weekday 07:00–10:00 window.", "Within the pilot, begin a controlled test in 10 of the 50 cafés: dynamically release any unused reserved café capacity to mobile orders if, after the first 60 minutes of peak, café demand is tracking below the 20% allocation (e.g., if less than 15% of capacity has actually been used for café orders by 08:00, release half of the remaining reserved slots for mobile pickup for the rest of the peak window)."], "expected_responses": ["Dutch Bros and Dunkin are likely to continue their current promotional tactics, as Starbucks has not signaled a major policy shift or price response. They may monitor for any indication that mobile order reliability improves or worsens.", "If the dynamic release test is successful, competitors may eventually copy or counter-message around digital convenience, but within this round, no immediate escalation is expected.", "Some habitual mobile customers may experience improved slot availability in the 10 test cafés, potentially reducing abandonment or competitive defection; café customers should not experience increased wait times if the release rule is triggered only when café demand is low."], "rationale": "Maintaining the original reservation policy is necessary to gather enough paired-store and customer repeat data to evaluate the effect on wait times and contribution, as required by the round-two decision rules. However, early evidence may reveal that the 20% café reservation is not fully utilized in some cafés or time intervals, risking unnecessary lost mobile transactions. Dynamically releasing unused reserved capacity in a subset of cafés allows us to test if we can recapture mobile volume without harming the café experience, while still observing the impact on both channels. This approach aligns with the incentive to defend transaction momentum and all-channel contribution, while remaining within staffing and scope constraints.", "resource_commitments": ["Continue incremental staffing (up to 2 additional peak staff-hours per weekday) in all 50 pilot cafés.", "Allocate digital and ops resources to implement and monitor the dynamic release rule in 10 pilot cafés (no new budget, but requires coordination and instrumentation updates)."]}, "content_hash": "9e93b6600c362a85f097f2f44349b29d5ea627deae7a7e4b1820d49acb136219", "move": 2, "provenance": {"answer_hash": "9e93b6600c362a85f097f2f44349b29d5ea627deae7a7e4b1820d49acb136219", "ingested_at": "2026-09-12T12:16:54.257428+00:00", "job_id": "job-659a154c465c4aadb5fde58f36a30226", "manifest_hash": "e691b8fc47dcb78b5801f754fb66194bbbced9d6229825a3c23bb8118d050ed5", "model": "gpt-4.1", "model_parameters": {"edsl_class_name": "LanguageModel", "edsl_version": "1.0.8.dev1", "inference_service": "openai", "model": "gpt-4.1", "parameters": {"frequency_penalty": 0, "logprobs": false, "max_tokens": 16000, "presence_penalty": 0, "reasoning_effort": null, "temperature": 0.5, "top_logprobs": 3, "top_p": 1}}, "origin": "simulation", "source_package": "/Users/johnhorton/tools/ep/perla/examples/starbucks-queue/dated-live/execution/round-2-moves-home/results-1.ep"}}], "testimony": []}

Morning customers responds

r2-buyer-behavior: accept. This ruling accurately reflects the different motivations and choices of our various customer segments—habitual app users, café visitors, and time-pressed commuters—based on their experiences in January.

r2-dunkin-actions: accept. We see the new breakfast bundle offer from Dunkin' in the market. We will evaluate it based on our individual needs for convenience, taste, and price on any given morning.

r2-dutch-actions: accept. The continuation of the Dutch Bros Order Ahead offer is noted. For those of us who have switched or are considering it, this remains an attractive option, especially when we're in a hurry.

r2-home-actions: accept. We don't know the internal rules Starbucks uses, but we will experience the results. We will continue to check the app for pickup times and observe the wait times in the café, and make our daily decisions based on that.

When competitors like Dutch Bros and Dunkin' make it easy and cheap to try their service, it's a logical time to explore new routines. Round closure receipt

Round 3 · March 2027: expand the test

March exposes the tension between improving an offer and repairing a changed habit. Starbucks expands its dynamic-release rule from 10 to all 50 pilot cafés, retaining the original 20% reservation and staffing cap. Dutch Bros keeps the $1 acquisition offer and adds a local review of lane times, order volume and repeat visits. Dunkin increases its proposed bundle discount to $1.50, splitting its $20,000 envelope equally between labor and marketing/promotional activity.

The customer model now says some formerly habitual Starbucks app users open a rival app by default; café visitors remain attached to the pilot stores, while commuters keep checking the daily pickup promise. This is a concrete strategic risk hypothesis: restoring availability may not immediately restore a routine that a customer has already changed. It is not an estimate of how many real customers would switch, and the model’s confidence about established habits exceeds the operating evidence available here.

Starbucks also proposes a rollback rule if mobile abandonment or café waits worsen by “more than 5 percentage points” against paired controls. That phrasing is usable for a rate such as abandonment, but a wait measured in minutes needs a time-unit or relative-percent threshold. The returned move is preserved exactly. Control’s structural acceptance does not fix the unit ambiguity, and expanding the variation across the pilot still lacks measured support from its ten-store trial.

All four actors accept the integrated March ruling, and control affirms it. The board reaches March and records the expanded pilot variation, rival offers and assumed customer routines. The repeated agreement is a finding about these model responses; it supplies no additional operating evidence. Six judgment rulings across the three rounds remain without human assessments. No final criterion evaluation has been executed, and the required observed waits, contribution and repeat data remain absent.

These move packages use the board produced by the previous closed round. The players receive that public situation and their original dossiers, so visible changes must be carried forward explicitly. They do not receive an unrestricted private conversation history.

Recorded model gameplay · Round 3 · March 2027

Starbucks’s move

Played by gpt-4.1 · openai

01 / Presented to the model

Task instruction · verbatim excerpt

Play only the actor whose dossier is supplied. Choose a committed strategic move consistent with its incentives, constraints, and available resources. State concrete actions, the rationale, resource commitments, and expected competitor responses.

Also supplied: the proposed decision, the public situation entering round 3 and Starbucks’s own dossier. Other players’ uncommitted moves were withheld. Read the complete input.

02 / Returned by the model

Committed actions · verbatim

Continue the 20% peak café capacity reservation and mobile order limits in all 50 pilot cafés during weekday 7–10 a.m. through March 2027.

Expand the dynamic release of unused reserved slots (after 08:00 if café demand is below 15% of capacity) from 10 to all 50 pilot cafés, with real-time monitoring for adverse mobile order abandonment or in-café congestion.

Set a pre-commitment to rollback the dynamic slot release in any pilot café if measured mobile order abandonment or in-café wait times worsen by more than 5 percentage points versus paired controls.

Model’s rationale · verbatim

The continued 20% reservation aligns with the strategic objective to protect the in-café experience for core customers, as the coffeehouse visit is central to the Starbucks proposition (h1, h4). Expanding the dynamic release of unused reserved slots system-wide after 08:00 leverages observed lower in-café demand in late peak windows, aiming to recapture mobile transactions that might otherwise divert to competitors. This approach balances the need to defend transaction momentum (h3) and earn back added labor by maximizing capacity utilization without breaching the operational or staffing constraints (h5, h6). The explicit rollback rule addresses the requirement for reversibility and safeguards against negative contribution or excessive churn (h9).

Model’s resource commitments and expected responses · verbatim

Resource commitments

Maintain incremental staffing up to 2 peak hours per weekday per pilot café, within the existing cap.

Deploy digital instrumentation and real-time monitoring for mobile order abandonment, café wait times, and slot utilization in all 50 pilot cafés.

Allocate operations and analytics resources to enforce the rollback rule at the café level if negative impacts are detected.

Expected responses

Dutch Bros and Dunkin may intensify local app offers if they observe Starbucks relaxing mobile slot limits, but may also see reduced switching if Starbucks improves mobile reliability.

Competitors may adjust their labor or promotional spend in response to any perceived Starbucks vulnerability in mobile or café service.

Some habitual Starbucks app users may return if their mobile order experience improves, while café-first customers should not see degraded wait times.
